258	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
259	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
260	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
261	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
262	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
263	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
264	
265	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
266	
267	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
268	
269	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
270	
271	## Writing to the record
272	
273	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
274	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
275	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
276	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
277	  - what it means for the work;
278	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
279	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
280	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
281	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
282	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
283	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
284	
285	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
286	
287	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
288	
289	To add a row:
290	
291	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
292	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
293	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
294	
295	To change a row:
296	
297	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N.
298	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
299	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it.
300	
301	## The repository's history
302	
303	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
304	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
305	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
306	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
307	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
308	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
309	# The specification
310	
311	Three folders hold the team's specification:
312	
313	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
314	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
315	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
316	
317	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
318	
319	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
320	
321	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
322	
323	To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".
324	
325	## Changing the text: the revision form
326	
327	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
328	
329	1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
330	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
331	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
332	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
333	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
334	
335	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
336	
337	2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:
338	
339	       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}
340	
341	   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.
342	
343	3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
344	
345	4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.
346	
347	If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.
348	
349	Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.
350	
351	## Building it
352	
353	To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):
354	
355	    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
356	
357	- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'Reference .* undefined\|multiply defined\|Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
358	- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
359	- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
360	- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.
361	
362	## When the text and an implementation disagree
363	
364	- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
365	- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
366	- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.
367	
368	## Citing it
369	
370	- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
371	- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.

14	## 1. What changed, and why
15	
16	**Rows 727, 572 and 734: the per-provider check reads abstract functional methods.** Q1's answer is (a), refuse (P-149). `toFunctionalMethodArrows` now keeps every functional method a trait or object provides, as `toMethodArrows` keeps every dotted one (`OverloadingChecker.scala:131-137`). It keeps the `implemented` filter, which drops an abstract method that a declaration of a strict subtype with the same parameter types implements (`:147-152`). Before, in a component, it kept a functional method only if the method had a body or its trait came from an imported api (`:138-141` at the base). That was the judge's reading (b) of climb batch 8 (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-overloading-checker/JUDGE.md`, section 7, decision 1). The revival's helper `declaredInUnit`, used only by that condition, is removed (`:173-181` at the base).

On the base, an object's own `f(self): String` that defines its trait's abstract `f(self): ZZ32` compiled, and its run failed with 'java.lang.VerifyError: Bad return type'. The dotted twin was refused. The return-type check of an overriding pair reads its arrows through the same function (`OverloadingChecker.scala:657-658`), so it now refuses the functional one too: 'For f, the return type of O->String ... should be a subtype of the return type of T->ZZ32'.

1	# Rung K (`rung-checker-abstract-callsite`): record lines for the gather
2	
3	Written by the rung worker for the gather's fold. `<K1>` is 96c441771 (the overloading change and the first version of the place) and `<K3>` is a79a51661 (the final rule for the place), on `wip/rung-checker-abstract-callsite`. The gather puts in the landed hashes.
4	
5	## FACTS.md
6	
7	Rewrite F-80, in "The checker and the one library". Its "Unchecked" part is false since `<K1>`:
8	
9	- F-80 **The compiled checker judges two functional methods of one name by the Meet Rule for Functional Methods, in each type that provides both, abstract declarations included, and keys its overloading memo on the check's inputs.** Such a type must provide their meet, compared without the self parameter. F-88 says what a type provides. An abstract functional method beside a concrete one with the same parameter type is refused by the No Duplicates Rule. Unchecked: a pair that only an object expression provides (row 570). Gated by `compiler_tests/FunctionalMethodMeet*`, `XXXFunctionalMethodMeetAbstractSibling` and `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstract`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-overloading-checker/REPORT.md` section 5; `compile-ladder/rung-checker-abstract-callsite/REPORT.md` section 1.
10	
11	A new entry, in "The checker and the one library":
12	
13	- **The well-formedness walk reports an ill-formed type that it meets outside the expression it is in at that expression, so a call whose static argument breaks the bound of the callee's result type is reported at the call.**
14	  - A call's type keeps the spans of the callee's declared type.
15	  - An error on such a type is reported once for each message and place the type would give, at the innermost expression the walk met it in.
16	  - Where the type is ill-formed where it is written, its error stays at the declaration.
17	  - So no error is added or dropped: the count stays 39 and the distance 49, and row 433's two fusion-pair sites are at their calls, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3422` and `:3424`.
18	  - Source: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:42-82`.
19	  - Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXStaticArgBoundAtCall`, `XXXStaticArgBoundAtCallOnce` and `XXXIllFormedTypeAtDeclarationOnce`.
20	  - Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-abstract-callsite/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 6.
21	
22	## Ledger notes and closes
23	
24	- **Row 727**: close with `ledger.py close 727 --commit <K1> --test XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstract`. Note: "fixed <K1> (climb batch 16 rung K): the per-provider set reads a type's abstract functional methods (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:137`), 'There are multiple declarations of f with the same parameter type: (S)'; the pair at two self positions is `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstractSelfPositions`."
25	- **Row 572**: close with `--commit <K1> --test XXXFunctionalMethodMeetAbstractSibling`. Note: "fixed <K1>: refused by the Meet Rule, 'Invalid overloading of pick in trait O'; walk refuses the shape at load (F-142), not by row 100's mechanism."
26	- **Row 734**: close with `--commit <K1> --test XXXFunctionalMethodMeetAbstractSiblingNarrower`. Note: "fixed <K1>: refused as row 572's shape, 'Invalid overloading of pick in trait O: A->R ... and B->R1'."
27	- **Row 720**: close with `--commit <K3> --test XXXStaticArgBoundAtCall`. Note: "fixed <K3>: reported at the call, once (`XXXStaticArgBoundAtCallOnce`); a type ill-formed where it is written keeps its error at the declaration (`XXXIllFormedTypeAtDeclarationOnce`); the reproducer's two errors are at its :16:20-17:8."
28	- **Row 433**, append: "Since <K3> (climb batch 16 rung K) its two wellformed sites, `MaxSumReductionPair[\T\]` and `MinSumReductionPair[\T\]`, are reported at the calls in `SumReduction`'s `distribute`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3422` and `:3424`, not at the objects' declarations `:3405` and `:3411`; the sites at `:3421` and `:3423` stay."
29	- **Row 707**, append: "Since <K1> an abstract `f(self, y: S)` beside a concrete `f(x: S, self)` reaches this check (`XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstractSelfPositions`)."
30	- **Row 726**, append: "Unchanged by <K1>, which reads abstract functional methods but no symbolic operator (row 584); `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsOperator` keeps its code-generator key."

34	## New rows
35	
36	In section 5, "Overloading on the compiled path: checker and dispatch":
37	
38	| NEW-K-1 | the compiled checker's per-provider overloading message calls every trait or object a trait: 'Invalid overloading of m in trait O' for `object O`, since its kind word tests the compilation unit where the trait or object is meant | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (checker) | silent | `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXDottedMethodMeetAbstractSibling.test` | climb batch 16 rung K | `traitKindAndName` matches `compilation_unit` against `ObjectTraitIndex` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:338` at a79a51661, a team line), which a compilation unit never is; the test pins today's text. The same word is in the refusals of rows 572, 734 and 735. Fix: match `traitOrObject`. |
39	
40	## Handover line
41	
42	Climb batch 16, rung K landed on `wip/rung-checker-abstract-callsite`:
43	- The compiled checker reads the abstract functional methods a type provides (P-149). Rows 727, 572 and 734 are closed, and an object's functional method that defines its trait's abstract one with an unrelated return type is refused.
44	- A call's ill-formed type is reported at the call, once. Row 720 is closed, and row 433's two sites are at `FortressLibrary.fss:3422` and `:3424`.
45	- Count 39 and distance 49, tables unchanged. Both libraries unchanged. Count seconds 383 and 367 on the base, 393 and 371 on the change.
46	- Appendix I's sentence on row 727 is corrected.
47	- New row NEW-K-1: the message calls an object 'trait'.
48	
49	## Revival change
50	
51	**The change.** There are two.
52	
53	1. **The overloading check of what a type provides.** The team's compiled checker of 2012 read only functional methods with a body when it checked the overloading of what a trait or object provides (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala`, line 133 at a874948ac). It did read abstract dotted methods (lines 144-146 there).
54	   - So an abstract functional method beside a concrete one with the same parameter type, in one trait, passed the checker and stopped the code generator.
55	   - An object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and a body from another, and declares none of its own, compiled and ran the body.
56	   - An object's functional method that defines its trait's abstract one with an unrelated return type compiled and failed verification: 'java.lang.VerifyError: Bad return type'.
57	
58	   The tree now reads every functional method a type provides. It refuses the first, 'There are multiple declarations of f with the same parameter type' (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstract.test`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstractSelfPositions.test`). It refuses the second, 'Invalid overloading of pick in trait O' (`XXXFunctionalMethodMeetAbstractSibling.test`, `XXXFunctionalMethodMeetAbstractSiblingNarrower.test`). It refuses the third, 'For f, the return type of ... should be a subtype of ...' (`XXXAbstractFunctionalMethodReturnType.test`).
59	
60	   The reason:
61	   - the No Duplicates Rule (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:548-549`);
62	   - the Meet Rule over what a type provides, abstract declarations included (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:580-581`);
63	   - the rule that an object defines each abstract method it inherits (`traits.tex:628-633`);
64	   - the code generator's own refusal of such a set, 'Likely bug in static analysis, apparently malformed overload set not rejected' (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:409-411`);
65	   - walk refuses all three shapes at load.
66	
67	2. **Where a type's error is reported.** The team's well-formedness walk reported an error on a type at the type's own node (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TypeWellFormedChecker.scala`, line 113 at a874948ac). A call's type keeps the spans of the callee's declared type, so a call whose static argument breaks the bound of the callee's result type was reported at the callee's declaration.
68	
69	   The tree reports it at the call (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXStaticArgBoundAtCall.test`), once (`XXXStaticArgBoundAtCallOnce.test`). It keeps at the declaration the error of a type that is ill-formed where it is written (`XXXIllFormedTypeAtDeclarationOnce.test`).
70	
71	   The reason, as evidence:
72	   - The old place holds no error of its own. On the old code `XXXStaticArgBoundAtCall` names its line 12, `vec`'s declared result, which is well-formed in `vec`'s scope; the call with the unbounded argument is on line 13.
73	   - The library's two such errors named the objects' declarations, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3405` and `:3411`, whose bounds are their own. The unbounded argument is written at the calls `:3422` and `:3424`.
74	
75	**Provenance.**
76	- The first change follows Q1 of climb batch 16 (review-queue item 62), answered (a), refuse (P-149), for rows 727 and 572; row 734 closes with them.
77	- The second follows the coordinator's call 4 of climb batch 16, for row 720.
78	- Both are climb batch 16, rung K.

55	   - (a) Every declaration, abstract included, with the `implemented` filter. This is closest to the letter of "provides". 187	\paragraph{\KWD{getter}:}
188	A method declaration with the modifier \KWD{getter} explicitly declares a

190	\note{The following description is too confusing.  Reword it!!!}

207	setter method for a field, even in the absence of an actual field.
208	\note{The following description is too confusing.  Reword it!!!}
209	If such a field exists, there is no implicit setter for the field.
210	An explicitly declared setter method must take a single argument---the
211	value being set---and return \EXP{()}.
212	A setter method must not throw any checked exception.

content.content:
That paper's soundness proof excludes an upper bound that names a type
parameter, its own included, and closed types, so that \library's families over a type parameter
bounded by an instance of a trait at itself, such as \STR{SUM}, \STR{BIG~MAX}
and those over \TYP{Integral}, rest on the rules of 2011 as the compiled type
checker implements them, and not on the proof of 2019.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
The No Duplicates Rule was first stated on the strict sense of more specific
that the section defines, under which no two declarations are each more
specific than the other, so that it refused no pair, and two declarations each
applicable to every call to which the other is fell to the Meet Rule (row~696
of the revival's gap ledger).
The paper of 2011 defines its relation of specificity without strictness, one
declaration being more specific than another when every type to which the first
is applicable is one to which the second is, and its No Duplicates Rule
``forbids distinct declarations from being equally specific''
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 97--108, 158--162 and 184--185);
the paper of 2019 states it as ``Distinct method declarations must have
different applicable sets'' (Section~2.2), and its rules [No-Dup-Not-Less] and
[No-Dup-Not-Gtr] refuse exactly a pair whose domain types are each a subtype of
the other (Section~4.1 and Figure~5).
The restatement follows the revival's decision of 23~September 2026 that the
type group's later word, that paper among it, outweighs the early text; its
reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-popl-examples/REPORT.md} in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] Declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters,
as \library's do.
The compiled type checker refuses the pair of the Return Type Rule's example,
which it accepted before and whose compiled class then failed verification, and
an override whose return type reorders its static parameters, which it accepted
before and which then failed at run time (row~398).
Neither implementation runs every set these rules allow.
The compiled type checker refuses more than the Return Type Rule where the more
specific declaration's parameter type is an object type, as in
\EXP{\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T} beside
\EXP{\VAR{ident}(x\COLON \TYP{Circle})\COLON \TYP{Circle}} where \TYP{Circle} is an
object (row~542); the compiled code generator fails on two declarations with
static parameters whose bounds differ, the pair the Return Type Rule allows in
\secref{overloading-static-params} among them, and on the example of the type
group's paper of 2019 that overloads a method over an array list and a list
(row~537); and the interpreter refuses at load two declarations with static
parameters of which no pair of parameter types excludes each other (row~159),
that example among them (row~539).
Jan's example is still not a valid overloading, its two declarations having the
same parameter type.
The compiled type checker applies the No Duplicates Rule as it is now stated:
it refuses two declarations whose parameter types, read over their instances,
are each a subtype of the other, ``There are multiple declarations of \VAR{dup}
with the same parameter type'', two functional methods among them wherever their
\KWD{self} parameters stand.
It reads the abstract functional methods that a trait or object provides as it
reads the abstract dotted ones, so that an abstract functional method beside a
concrete one with the same parameter type is among the pairs it refuses, which
only its code generator refused before, as a malformed overload set.
It checks no overloading of an operator whose name is not a word of capitals
(row~584 of the revival's gap ledger): two declarations of such an operator with
the same parameter type pass it, and only its code generator refuses them, as a
malformed overload set (row~726).
The interpreter loads such a pair and runs one of them where both declarations
have static parameters and their parameter types mention one parameterized
type, as \VAR{dup}'s do (row~373), and where one has static parameters and the
other's parameter type is its bound (row~549).
The calculus of \appref{overloading-calculus} keeps its rule that two
declarations with the same number of parameters have static parameters with the
same bounds; it admits fewer overloadings than these chapters, so that its valid
programs are still valid, and its rules and its soundness claim are unchanged
(\secref{revival-calculi}).
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/overloading.tex},
lines 100--108:
\begin{quote}
Although there may be multiple declarations with the same functional name,
it is an error for their static parameters to differ (up to
$\alpha$-equivalence), or for one declaration to have static parameters and
another to not have them.
Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which
declarations are applicable, so we ignore them for most of this chapter.
\end{quote}
lines 137--138:
\begin{quote}
We assume throughout this chapter that all static variables in functional calls
have been instantiated or inferred.
\end{quote}
lines 173--175, and in the same words for the types $\Ps_0$ and $\Ps$ of a
dotted method declaration, lines 205--207:
\begin{quote}
If the parameter type $\Ps$ includes static parameters, they are inferred as
described in \chapref{type-inference} before checking the applicability of the
declaration to the call.
\end{quote}

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table was produced, 1 if it could not be. 20 s in the main tree,
# measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The two sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-22 from
# explorations/perf-probes/prelude/, so that the gate does not depend on a probe
# directory: WorldFlip.java (Shell.useInterpreterLibraries() plus
# PhaseOrder.compilerPhaseOrder, both public, which is the world switch without an edit
# to a tracked file) and shadow-src/.../StaticChecker.java, a copy of
# ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java with three
# instrumentation points added: it names each compilation unit it checks and prints that
# unit's error count, and it catches the OverloadingChecker crash instead of dying on it.
# It is put AHEAD of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath, the technique of
# perf-probes/prelude/run-all.sh:33-35. A copy of a tracked source goes stale silently,
# so the checksum of the tracked one is recorded here and the table's "#shadow" line
# says whether it still matches.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false, read
# at OverloadingChecker.scala:77), since 2026-09-27 (climb batch 7). The memo is keyed on
# declaration pairs and hides 27 to 35 errors depending on the build order once an api's
# overloading check runs (perf-probes/nat/triage.md section 1; FACTS.md, "The hidden
# layer, classified"); with it off every build gives one count. The table's "#cache"
# row says so. On the tree of 2026-09-27 the count is 62 with the memo on and off,
# because the FortressLibrary api stops before its overloading check.
set -u

STOCK_SHA=16e6e11df9341a67038b7d7cc9f0d7bb5e5a6149019f09e92545a8b646363a0b   # ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java, 2026-09-22

OUT=${1:-}
if [ -z "$OUT" ] ; then echo "usage: $0 <out-file> [scratch-dir]" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi
case "$OUT" in /*) ;; *) OUT="$PWD/$OUT" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
D="$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count"
TARGET=Library/FortressLibrary.fss
SCRATCH=${2:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/checker-count.$$}
STOCK=$FH/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java
OVERLOAD_CACHE=false     # the overloading checker's memo, off: see the header

mkdir -p "$SCRATCH/classes" "$SCRATCH/caches" "$(dirname "$OUT")" || exit 1
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
if [ -z "$CP" ] ; then echo "checker-count: no classpath from bin/fortress_classpath" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi

cat > SkValidAbstract.fss <<'EOF'
component SkValidAbstract
export Executable
trait Shape
  area(self): ZZ32
  scale(self, k: ZZ32): ZZ32
  scale(self, s: String): String
end
trait Named extends Shape
  name(self): String = "named"
end
object Sq(s: ZZ32) extends Named
  area(self): ZZ32 = s s
  scale(self, k: ZZ32): ZZ32 = k s
  scale(self, t: String): String = t
end
trait Box[\T\]
  holds(self, x: T): Boolean
end
object IntBox(v: ZZ32) extends Box[\ZZ32\]
  holds(self, x: ZZ32): Boolean = (x = v)
end
run(): () = do
  q: Shape = Sq(3)
  b: Box[\ZZ32\] = IntBox(4)
  assert(area(q), 9, "area")
  assert(scale(q, 2), 6, "scale")
  assert(scale(q, "s"), "s", "scale s")
  assert(holds(b, 4), "holds")
  assert(NOT holds(b, 5), "holds 5")
  println("PASS")
end
end
EOF

component SkCovering

  f(self, k: K): ZZ32
end

  f(self, p: P): ZZ32 = 1
  f(self, q: Q): ZZ32 = 2
end
run(): () = do
  t: T = O
  assert(f(t, P), 1, "P")
  assert(f(t, Q), 2, "Q")
  println("PASS")
end
end
EOF

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The specification's revision

POSITIONS.md:97
- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** No discrepancy between the specification and the implementation stays open to confuse a reader. The original text and the reasons are kept, so that route C, the way back to the patents' forest rule (P-43), stays open. Every change takes the S1 form (P-96). `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is never touched.

POSITIONS.md:98
- P-96 **The S1 form: a change of the specification is shown in the layered form that the team used for 1.0 and its 2009 draft.** A callout that prints in every build, not a `\note`, marks each changed passage. Appendix I's revival section gives each change its reason, its original text, the way back to route C and the decision it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a repository document holds the full reasoning. The unrevised copy is cited as the Working Draft of February 2011. The parts in detail: fortress-repo skill, `references/specification.md`.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:64
- P-149 **An object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from a sibling trait, and declares none of its own, is refused (Q1).** So `object O extends { A, B }`, with `pick(self)` abstract in `A` and given a body in `B`, must declare its own `pick`, as the specification's text and the type group's Welterweight calculus require and as walk already does; an abstract and a concrete declaration of one method in one trait are refused too. Why: the revival honors the designers' intent and does not change Fortress's nature for a convenience; other languages are consulted only to reconcile a conflict between earlier and later designers' choices, and here there is none. No library type uses the shape. Still to build: climb batch 16's rung K, rows 572 and 727.

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## The checker and the one library

FACTS.md:73
- F-80 **The compiled checker judges two functional methods of one name by the Meet Rule for Functional Methods, in each type that provides both, and keys its overloading memo on the check's inputs.** Such a type must provide their meet, compared without the self parameter. F-88 says what a type provides. Unchecked: a pair one of whose declarations is the component's own abstract one (row 572), and a pair that only an object expression provides (row 570). Gated by `compiler_tests/FunctionalMethodMeet*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-overloading-checker/REPORT.md` section 5.

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## Landed semantics

FACTS.md:142
- F-142 **Walk checks at load the Meet Rule for Functional Methods per providing type, and gives a type parameter that an argument bounds only from above its interval's upper end.** The meet check covers every trait, object and object expression, a generic one through a stand-in (F-145). A type provides what it declares and what it inherits, but not what its `override` declarations override. Symbolic operators are skipped, as the checker skips them (row 611). Walk's other refusals at load are in the `fortress-repo` skill's `references/interpreter.md`. Gated by `tests/FunctionalMethodMeet*` and `InferContravariantWalk`. Residues: rows 611, 612 and 616. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-meet/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 7.

\paragraph{The Meet Rule for Dotted Methods:}
Suppose that $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ and $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ are two dotted method
declarations provided by a trait or object $C$ such that neither
$(\Ps_0, \Ps)$ nor $(\Qs_0, \Qs)$ is a subtype of the other and $\Ps$
and $\Qs$ are not incompatible with one another.
Let $\mathpzc{S}$ be the set of
types that $\Ps$ defines coercions from and $\mathpzc{T}$ be the set
of types that $\Qs$ defines coercions from.
$\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ and
$\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ are a valid overloading if
there is a declaration $\Rs_0.\f(\Ps
\inter \Qs)$ provided by $C$ with $\Rs_0 \Ovrsubtype (\Ps_0 \inter
\Qs_0)$.

\item
either $\Ps \excludes \Qs$ or there is a declaration $\Rs_0.\f(\Ps
\inter \Qs)$ provided by $C$ with $\Rs_0 \Ovrsubtype (\Ps_0 \inter
\Qs_0)$, and
\item
either $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$ or $\Qs \morespecific \Ps$ or
for all $\Ps' \in \mathpzc{S}$ and
$\Qs' \in \mathpzc{T}$ one of the two conditions holds:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$\Ps' \excludes \Qs'$, or
\item
there is a declaration $\Rs_0.\f(\Ps' \inter \Qs')$ provided by $C$
with $\Rs_0 \Ovrsubtype (\Ps_0 \inter \Qs_0)$.
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Recall that functional methods can be viewed semantically as top-level
functions, as described in \secref{methods}.  However, treating
functional methods as top-level functions for determining valid
overloading is too restrictive.  In the following example:
\input{\home/advanced/examples/Overloading.tex}
if the functional methods were interpreted as top-level functions then
this program would define two top-level functions with parameter types
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}}.
These declarations would be
statically rejected as
an invalid overloading because there is no
relation between \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}}; another trait
may extend them both without declaring its own version of the
functional method which may lead to an ambiguous call at run time.
However, notice that declaraions are ambiguous only for calls on
arguments that extend both \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}}, and
any type that extends both can include a new declaration that
disambiguates them.  We use this intuition to allow such overloadings.

\paragraph{The Meet Rule for Functional Methods:}
Suppose that $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are two functional method
declarations occurring in trait or object declarations or object expressions
such that neither $\Ps$ nor $\Qs$ is a subtype of the other and $\Ps$ and $\Qs$
are not incompatible with one another.  Let $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$
have self parameters at $i$ and $j$ respectively.
$\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are a valid
overloading if all of the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$i = j$
\item if there exists a trait or object $C$
that provides both $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ then $\Ps \neq \Qs$ and
there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ provide by $C$
having self parameter at $i$.
\end{itemize}

Also, let $\mathpzc{S}$ be the set of types that $\Ps$
defines coercions from and $\mathpzc{T}$ be the set of types that
$\Qs$ defines coercions from.  $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are a valid
overloading if all of the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$i = j$
\item
either $\Ps \excludes \Qs$ or if there exists a trait or object $C$
that provides both $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ then $\Ps \neq \Qs$ and
there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ provide by $C$, and
\item
either $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$ or $\Qs \morespecific \Ps$ or
for all $\Ps' \in \mathpzc{S}$ and
$\Qs' \in \mathpzc{T}$ one of the two conditions holds:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$\Ps' \excludes \Qs'$, or
\item
there is a declaration $\f(\Ps' \inter \Qs')$ provided by $C$.
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

As for functions, where this rule asks for a declaration
$\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ provided by $C$, it is also satisfied by declarations
provided by $C$, having self parameter at $i$, whose parameter types are each a
subtype of both $\Ps$ and $\Qs$ and together cover $\Ps \inter \Qs$; the case
does not apply to the condition on the types from which $\Ps$ and $\Qs$ define
coercions.
\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 asked here, as for
functions, for a declaration on the intersection itself.}

Notice that the Meet Rule for functional methods requires the self
parameters of two overloaded declarations to be in the same position.
This requirement guarantees that no ambiguity is caused by the
position of the self parameter.  Two declarations which differ in the
position of the self parameter must satisfy either the Subtype Rule or
the Incompatibility Rule to be a valid overloading.

Functional method declarations can overload with function declaraions.
A valid overloading between a functional method declaration and
a function declaration is
determined by applying the (more restrictive) Meet Rule for functions
to both declarations.

#!/bin/bash
# old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...
#
# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
# deletes two empty, gitignored logs beside Library/Executable.fsi. Two runs at once may share those two
# names; that is harmless, because the base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty and
# a log removed by the other run reads as empty (Parser.java:373-377). Measured in
# explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, section 6.
#
# Keep the private folder and your programs outside the base build (the program's own logs go beside it).
# Refuses (exit 2) a base build that is not built, and a private folder inside the base build.
set -euo pipefail
USAGE='usage: old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...'
BASE=$(realpath "${1:?$USAGE}")
PRIV_ARG=${2:?$USAGE}
shift 2
[ -x "$BASE/bin/fortress" ] && [ -e "$BASE/ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class" ] \
  && [ -e "$BASE/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar" ] \
  || { echo "old-fortress: $BASE is not a built tree" >&2 ; exit 2 ; }
PRIV=$(realpath -m "$PRIV_ARG")
case "$PRIV/" in "$BASE"/*) echo "old-fortress: $PRIV is inside the base build $BASE" >&2 ; exit 2 ;; esac
if [ ! -d "$PRIV" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$PRIV")"
    PART="$PRIV.part.$$"
    cp -a "$BASE/default_repository/caches" "$PART"
    mv -T "$PART" "$PRIV" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "$PART"     # another run made it first: use that one

every argument type other than \TYP{BottomType} to which $d_1$ is applicable,
and for every instance of $d_2$ that is applicable to it, some instance of $d_1$
is applicable to it whose return type is a subtype of the return type of that
instance of $d_2$.
\end{itemize}

content.content:
# 1. build the driver and the instrumented checker against the tree's own classpath
javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d "$SCRATCH/classes" \
      "$D/WorldFlip.java" "$D/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java" \
      > "$SCRATCH/javac.txt" 2>&1
if [ $? -ne 0 ] ; then
    echo "checker-count: javac failed; see $SCRATCH/javac.txt" >&2 ; tail -20 "$SCRATCH/javac.txt" >&2 ; exit 1
fi

# 2. run the compiler phase order over the interpreter's library under a private cache
( cd "$FH" && timeout -k 10 900 java -Xmx4g -Xss64m -Dfortress.caches="$SCRATCH/caches" \
       -Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=$OVERLOAD_CACHE \
       -cp "$SCRATCH/classes:$CP" WorldFlip "$TARGET" ) > "$SCRATCH/run.txt" 2>&1
RC=$?
if ! grep -q 'has [0-9]* errors\?\.$' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" ; then
    echo "checker-count: the run printed no error total (rc=$RC); see $SCRATCH/run.txt" >&2
    tail -20 "$SCRATCH/run.txt" >&2 ; exit 1
fi

# 3. the table. One row per api the checker named, its own error count as the
#    instrumented checker printed it; then the total, the number of distinct
#    file:line the errors were reported at, and the first crash the checker
#    survived. Rows are sorted so that two runs of the same tree are byte-equal.
{
    printf '#api\terrors\n'
    grep '^@@PROBE checkApi .* -> errors=' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" \
        | sed -E 's/^@@PROBE checkApi ([^ ]+) -> errors=([0-9]+)$/\1\t\2/' | sort -u
    printf '#total\t%s\n' "$(grep -oE 'has [0-9]+ errors?\.$' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" | tail -1 | grep -oE '[0-9]+')"
    printf '#locations\t%s\n' "$(grep -oE '^/[^ ]+:[0-9]+:' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" | sort -u | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
    crash=$(grep -m1 '^@@PROBE OverloadingChecker CRASHED on ' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" | sed 's/^@@PROBE //')
    site=$(grep -m1 -A6 '^@@PROBE OverloadingChecker CRASHED on ' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" \
           | grep -oE '\([A-Za-z0-9_$]+\.(scala|java):[0-9]+\)' | grep -v '(NI\.java:' \
           | head -1 | tr -d '()')      # the first frame that is not the nyi helper itself
    printf '#crash\t%s\n' "${crash:-none}${site:+ at $site}"
    printf '#cache\toverloading memo %s (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=%s)\n' \
           "$( [ "$OVERLOAD_CACHE" = false ] && echo off || echo on )" "$OVERLOAD_CACHE"
    if [ "$(sha256sum < "$STOCK" | cut -d' ' -f1)" = "$STOCK_SHA" ] ; then
        printf '#shadow\tmatches the tracked StaticChecker\n'
    else
        printf '#shadow\tSTALE: ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java has changed since the copy was taken; refresh the copy and the checksum in run.sh\n'
    fi
} > "$OUT"

cat "$OUT"
echo "# checker-count: full output $SCRATCH/run.txt, rc=$RC"

content.content:
\item[Effect] The Meet Rule's example is valid; both implementations refused it
before this change (row~492 of the revival's gap ledger).
A static call whose argument's static type stands between two traits with
\KWD{comprises} clauses, as an instantiation of a trait with static parameters
that extends both unlisted does, is not a static error: it runs the declaration
that covers its value, and, where those declarations and every declaration more
specific than them that the call may run have no static parameters, its type is
the intersection of the return types of its most specific declarations.
The compiled type checker departs from this in four ways: it types such a call
by the intersection only in a family none of whose declarations has static
parameters, and otherwise by one of its most specific declarations (row~543 of
the revival's gap ledger); its code generator stops at a method call on a value
of such a type (row~540); it refuses the case for declarations with static
parameters (row~546); and its verdict on a trait between the two that provides
both declarations of a functional method can depend on the components it
compiled before (row~547).
The Meet Rule for dotted methods keeps its form, asking for a declaration on the
intersection (\secref{revival-notrevised}).
\item[Original text] The Working Draft's rules are unchanged, the cases being
added after them.
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced/overloading.tex}, lines 303--307,
the example's conclusion:
\begin{quote}
Because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
clause of $U$, any subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of $V$.  Thus,
$V = S \inter T$, and the declaration $f(V)$ ``disambiguates'' $f(S)$ and
$f(T)$, i.e., it is applicable to and more specific for any call to which both
$f(S)$ and $f(T)$ are applicable.
\end{quote}
and lines 460--468, the second fact and the sentence after the two:
\begin{quote}
If any declaration is applicable to a static call then there exists a single
most specific declaration that is applicable to the static call and a single
most specific declaration that is applicable to the corresponding dynamic call.

Moreover, we can prove that the most specific declaration that is applicable to
a dynamic call is more specific than the most specific declaration that is
applicable to the corresponding static call.
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}

content.content:
- F-223 **The specification's No Duplicates Rule is the papers' non-strict rule, and the compiled checker applies it, to functional methods wherever their `self` parameters stand.** Two declarations of one name may not each be applicable to every call to which the other is, as in the type group's papers of 2011 and 2019 (P-26). The checker refuses such a pair, two functional methods at different `self` positions among them: "There are multiple declarations of f with the same parameter type", naming the domain of the declaration written first. It checks no symbolic operator (row 584) and reads no abstract functional method of a trait the component declares (row 727); such a pair passes it and stops the code generator (rows 726 and 727). Walk runs one of such a pair in two shapes (rows 373 and 549). Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXNoDuplicatesRule`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositions` and `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsPlain`, the checker's departures by `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsOperator` and `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstract`, and walk's departure by `tests/XXXNoDuplicatesRuleWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-popl-examples/REPORT.md` section 4, its `SKEPTIC.md` section 2, and `compile-ladder/rung-duplicates-coverage/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 8.
28:- F-35 **The `FortressLibrary` api has 25 declarations with a dead size, a size parameter that occurs in no parameter type, return type or body.** They check clean (P-40). Where the component omits the dead size, the export checker reports the api's declaration missing. Six vector `DOT` and juxtaposition operators have this shape, `[\T, nat n, nat m, nat p\]` in the api and `[\T, nat n\]` in th
35:- F-42 **A unit's earlier error hides its overloading and return-type checks, and the checker refuses a local function's parameter left untyped.** `StaticChecker` runs the overloading rules only on a unit with no earlier error, so clearing an early error can raise a count (F-53). The checker refuses an untyped local function parameter, "Missing parameter type for i", as at top level (rows 620, 
46:- F-53 **The distance to the switch-over is 49 errors and the checker count is 39, at the last landed gate.** The distance counts the checker's errors in the interpreter's library, led by the sized arrays (F-54). The count stops where the checker crashes or meets an error it cannot pass; since row 680's repair (F-233) nothing stops it, so its 39 are the `FortressLibrary` component's own errors,
54:- F-61 **"Use FortressLibrary for the compiler too" is three steps, of which the checker's sizes and the tower's errors are done and the natives are PLAN's phase 4.** F-67 and F-131 hold the first two. F-53 holds what the checker still reports on the library. F-32 counts the native bindings. No minimal `Array` or `Vector` shim can serve the compiler: `FlatArrays` uses the whole array protocol, 
59:- F-66 **The checker-count stage's table, `gate/checker-count.txt`, lands with every batch beside the gate's `summary.txt`.** Its total at the last landed gate is F-53's count. The gate's step 8 compares it with the newest landed table. The total is never red on its own, since a fix can raise it and two rungs' changes do not add. The gate is red on a crash line no rung declared, a stale shadow 
88:- F-220 **`__bigOperator`'s local `body` is typed `body(i: I): L`, which walk runs since it no longer instantiates a big operator's static parameter at `BottomType`.** The checker count passes it (F-53). Gated by `tests/UnwrittenListMapComprehensionWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-elements/REPORT.md` section 6.

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

# Rung K, the skeptic's review

Head judged: `a79a51661` (the worker's last commit of code; `23bc16268` adds only its report and record from the run's journal). Head after: the commit of this file. Verdict: **contested**, one fix contested (section 5.2).

- The count stage, timed on the base build and on the worker's head in one session (section 2).

- The diff against the rung's section, the specification and P-149 (section 4).

The eight test components the rung adds and the two I add have no namesake in the test folders or `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`; `enclosingExpr`, `outside` and `within` are private, beside private namesakes in other classes (`TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:78`, `impls/Misc.scala:151`).

## 2. The count stage (P-148)

Machine: nproc 4, Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz, openjdk 25.0.4.1, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`. `ps aux` before each run showed another tree's probe and, for the second run, rung H's skeptic's count stage on its head.

    seconds 371

- The head is 3.1 % above the base, within the 6 % of `compiler.md`; the worker's pairs were +2.6 % and +1.1 %. The rung's declarations take no measurable time, as the worker's profile says.
- My two tables are equal by `diff` (`#total 39`, `#locations 38`, `#crash none`), and equal to the worker's `base`, `change` and `pass` tables.
- My head's `run.txt`, with the tree path masked, is byte-equal to the worker's `change3` run. Against the base the only difference is row 433's two sites, `FortressLibrary.fss:3405` and `:3411` gone, `:3422:5-26` and `:3424:5-26` come.

## 3. Test first

From the worker's transcript (`agent-a2e6db75c8ee1fc90.jsonl`):
- 13:14:30, call `5By7x8`: `junit.sh base` on the base's build, before any edit of code (the first at 13:17:48, call `Eg1DLA`; the first build at 13:18:48, `rWoMKs`): 'Saw wrong failure' for `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstract`, `XXXFunctionalMethodMeetAbstractSibling` and `XXXStaticArgBoundAtCall`, 'Tests run: 5,  Failures: 4,  Errors: 0', the dotted guard 'Saw expected failure'.

The order holds for every test the worker names.

## 4. The diff

**`toFunctionalMethodArrows`** (`OverloadingChecker.scala:131-153`). The body condition is gone and the `implemented` filter stays, as the rung's section and P-149 ask; `declaredInUnit`, the revival's, had no other caller. The dotted set reads abstract dotted methods with no filter (`:170-172`): the precedent. The overriding return-type check reads its arrows through the same function (`:657-659`), so it now sees an abstract functional method of a component's own trait; that is the return-type face the worker measured, and two more faces in section 6. `isDeclaredName` and `validOp` are untouched (row 584).

**The well-formedness walk** (`TypeWellFormedChecker.scala`). An error on a node outside the nearest expression goes to an expression. Two faults, each measured by a program of mine and fixed (section 5).

**Appendix I** (`changes.tex:2622-2629`). The corrected sentence says what the checker does now for named functional methods, and the next keeps the operators' half (rows 584, 726). It is true of the head.
